title: Share of visitors in Facebook/Instagram in-app browsers, and whether mobile breaks
pass: The in-app browser share is reported (FacebookApp, InstagramApp and any other in-app names in the browsers list, as share of sessions), and mobile sessions show script-error, error-click, dead-click and rage-click shares at or below desktop (byDevice).
fails: A large part of traffic arrives inside Meta's in-app browsers, and mobile sessions show more script errors, error clicks, dead clicks or rage clicks than desktop: the page paid clicks land on works worse where those clicks open.
validate: From the Clarity snapshot (store's own Clarity, last 3 days): sum sessions for in-app entries in browsers (FacebookApp, InstagramApp, plus TikTok or Snapchat in-app names if listed) and divide by total sessions. Compare byDevice mobile vs desktop on scriptErrors, errorClicks, deadClicks and rageClicks. The snapshot does not split behaviours by browser, so the card says the breakage signal is mobile-wide, not in-app-only. If byDevice is null, report the share only and mark the comparison unavailable. GA4 OAuth session source/medium can show how much of the same window is paid social, for context.
action: Forward to the developer: test the landing and product pages inside the Instagram and Facebook apps (open the link from a DM or a test ad), and fix errors and taps that do nothing on mobile.
done_when: Next 3-day snapshot shows mobile error and dead/rage-click shares at or below desktop, and a manual in-app test adds to cart without errors.
why_it_matters: Meta clicks open in the in-app browser; if mobile breaks there, CVR on paid social likely drops and CPA reads higher, and it is the site, not the ad.
selected_because: Pool had no snapshot-measurable point; in-app share plus mobile vs desktop breakage answers 'does paid traffic convert' from the store's own data.

title: Quick-backs on the top landing page
pass: The top landing page (most visits in topPages, matched to its byUrl row) has a quick-back share at or below the site-wide quickbacks.sessionsPct.
fails: Visitors land on the top landing page and bounce back to where they came from faster than on the rest of the site: the page does not match what the click promised, or loads into something they did not expect.
validate: From the Clarity snapshot: take topPages[0] (or the top non-home page if paid traffic lands on product or collection pages), find its byUrl row, and compare quickbacks % with behaviours.quickbacks.sessionsPct. If byUrl is null, mark unavailable. GA4 OAuth landing-page report filtered to paid source/medium names which page paid traffic actually lands on; use that page if it appears in byUrl. Our headless phone visit of the same page gives a screenshot of the first screen for the card.
action: Forward to the store owner: check that the top landing page's first screen shows the product and offer from the ad. If the ad sells one product, land on that product, not the home page.
done_when: Next 3-day snapshot shows the top landing page's quick-back share at or below the site average.
why_it_matters: Quick-backs on the page ads send traffic to likely mean paid clicks that never get a chance to convert, so CVR reads low and CAC high because of the page, not the targeting.
selected_because: Quick-backs on the landing page are the closest snapshot signal to post-click message mismatch, compared only with the store's own average.

title: Bot traffic inflating the session count
pass: GA4 sessions for the same 3 days are not above Clarity's sessions plus botSessions; Clarity's bot share (botSessions / (sessions + botSessions)) is reported.
fails: GA4 counts more sessions than Clarity saw in total, bots included, for the same days: GA4 is likely counting non-human or duplicate traffic that dilutes CVR and makes paid traffic look worse than it is.
validate: From the Clarity snapshot: botSessions and sessions give the bot share, reported as a fact. From GA4 OAuth: sessions for the same 3 dates (and by session source/medium for paid). Fail when GA4 sessions exceed Clarity sessions + botSessions. Note on the card: consent banners and ad blockers can make either tool undercount, so the result is direction only. Referrers in the snapshot can show whether paid-click referrers (facebook, instagram, google, snapchat, tiktok) are present at all.
action: Forward to whoever owns GA4: check the paid source/medium rows for sessions with no engagement and odd countries or hours, and exclude known bot traffic before judging CVR.
done_when: GA4 sessions for a 3-day window are at or below Clarity sessions plus bot sessions for the same window.
why_it_matters: Extra non-human sessions in GA4 push reported CVR down, so paid traffic can look like it converts worse than it does; the ad platforms' own counts are not checked here.
selected_because: Answers 'is the number real' on the traffic side by comparing two of the store's own tools, with no invented bot benchmark.
